points.text: The answer says that reckon.py's readers all take the log through log.read — the one place the file is parsed — so the tolerant, setting-aside reading lands once, at that seam, and covers those reckonings at a stroke rather than being built into each reader separately.

The answer says that monthend.py opens and parses the log file on its own rather than through log.read, so hardening log.read alone leaves the month-end carry still stopped by a bad line — the carry must be brought through the one gate, or hardened as a piece of its own, and the plan says which.

The answer says that log.rewrite writes the file whole, in place, so a failure partway through leaves the log holding less than it held, and the safe-write piece — writing aside and swapping, or keeping a copy first — is a piece of its own, separate from the reading side and workable independently of it.

The answer says that the log is one JSON object per line, appended a line at a time, so damage comes by the line rather than by the file, and setting a bad line aside while the rest are reckoned is possible exactly because of that format.

The answer says that the readers index fields straight out of each line — the day, the working, the quarters — so a line that parses as JSON but lacks a field stops a reckoning just as an unparseable one does, and what log.read promises its callers about a set-aside line is a contract decided once for every reader.

disqualifiers.text: The answer claims that catching failures at the command line — wrapping the steward's commands so no error escapes — is by itself enough to meet the ruling, with the modules below needing no work of their own.
